title: Most of a company's bytes are old, cold, and undeletable
body: At a big company, most stored bytes are not profiles or messages. They are old photos, old logs and huge analytics tables. The typical pattern: written once, read heavily for a short time, then almost never read again. Yet you cannot just delete them. Some data trains machine learning models, some is needed for audits, and some is a user's wedding photo from 2012. Managing this mass of cooling data cheaply, without losing it, is the problem this chapter tackles.
deeper:
The chapter splits the problem into three parts. First, the data lake: the storage that sits under analytics, where engines scan huge tables. Second, tiering: moving data to cheaper media as it cools, so the small hot fraction stays on fast hardware while the large cold fraction sits on dense, cheap hardware. Third, archival: keeping data for decades at the lowest possible cost, where retrieval in hours is acceptable.

A fourth theme ties them together: retention, which decides how long data lives at all. Table formats such as Iceberg, Hudi and Delta come up repeatedly, but only briefly; the focus stays on the storage underneath them. The key mental shift is that storage economics is not about the average byte. It is about recognizing that most bytes are cold, that they get cold quickly, and that each temperature deserves different media, different redundancy and even different datacenter designs. The running example throughout is a global app with 1 billion users generating event logs, database snapshots and photos.

quiz.q: Why can't a company simply delete data once it stops being read often?
quiz.a: Cold data still has value or obligations: it may train ML models, be required for audits or compliance, or be irreplaceable user content like old personal photos.

section: 7.1 What a data lake really is
title: A data lake: shared files in columnar formats, many engines
body: A data lake is a large, shared store of raw and processed data files. The files are usually in open columnar formats such as Parquet or ORC, which store each column together so a query reads only the columns it needs. Many compute engines, including Spark, Presto/Trino, Hive and Flink, read and write the same files. Because the formats are open and shared, one copy of the data can serve many different tools and teams.
deeper:
Columnar layout is what makes lake scans affordable. If a table has 200 columns and a query needs three, a row-oriented file forces the engine to read all 200; a columnar file lets it fetch only the three column chunks. Columns also compress well because values of the same type and similar content sit next to each other, which is why encodings like run-length and dictionary work so effectively.

The shared, open nature matters as much as the layout. Because Spark, Trino, Hive and Flink all understand Parquet and ORC, a batch job can write a table that an interactive query engine reads minutes later, with no export step. That is different from a traditional warehouse, where data lives inside one vendor's engine. The trade-off is that someone must manage the files themselves: how big they are, which ones belong to a table, and when old ones are deleted. Much of this chapter is about those storage-level chores, such as small files, compaction and tiering, that the lake's openness pushes onto the platform team.

quiz.q: Why does storing data in a columnar format like Parquet make analytics queries cheaper?
quiz.a: Each column is stored together, so a query reads only the columns it needs instead of whole rows, and similar values compress better.

section: 7.1 What a data lake really is
title: Separate storage from compute and let clusters come and go
body: The key idea of a data lake is separation of storage and compute. All files sit in one big storage system, while compute clusters that process them come and go independently. You can add another query engine, or spin up a temporary cluster for a big job, without copying the data anywhere. Storage grows with how much data you keep; compute grows with how much work you run. Each can be sized and paid for on its own.
deeper:
Without separation, capacity planning gets awkward. If every storage server is also a compute server, a team that needs more disk but not more CPU still has to buy both, and vice versa. Separation removes that coupling: storage can be dense, disk-heavy machines or an object store, and compute can be ephemeral clusters that exist only while a job runs.

The cost is that every read crosses the network, because the data no longer sits on the machine doing the work. This became acceptable as datacenter networks grew fast and flat, and because columnar formats cut how many bytes each query must pull. Separation also lets many engines share the same data. A new engine does not need its own copy, which avoids drift between duplicated datasets and saves the storage bill. This idea explains the whole arc of the chapter: first-generation HDFS lakes tied storage and compute together, and the move to object stores and systems like Tectonic was largely about breaking that tie.

quiz.q: What does separating storage from compute let a team do that a combined design makes hard?
quiz.a: Scale disk and CPU independently, run ephemeral compute clusters, and add new query engines without copying data, paying only for what each side needs.

section: 7.1 What a data lake really is
title: Lakes are built for throughput and cost per byte, not latency
body: In the running example of a global app with 1 billion users, the lake holds three kinds of data. Event logs record every click, view and message-send, append-only, at many petabytes per year. Daily snapshots of the profile and message databases are copied in for analysis. Derived tables hold results like daily active users, ad reports and ML training sets. Nobody needs a single event in 5 ms, but analysts scan billions of rows per second.
deeper:
This workload shapes every design choice. Because the unit of work is a scan over billions of rows rather than a lookup of one record, the lake is optimized for throughput, measured in bytes per second, and for cost per byte. Latency for a single item hardly matters.

That is the opposite of a serving database, where a user waits on each request and milliseconds count. It frees the lake to use dense hard drives, aggressive erasure coding, network reads instead of local reads, and large files that are efficient to stream. It also explains why small files hurt so much: a lake tuned for streaming big sequential reads suffers when forced to issue millions of tiny requests. The three data types also age differently. Event logs grow endlessly and cool quickly. Snapshots are replaced daily. Derived tables may be rebuilt or read repeatedly. Those differences later drive different tiering and retention rules for each type, such as deleting raw click events after a couple of years.

quiz.q: Why is a data lake optimized for throughput rather than latency?
quiz.a: Its work is scanning billions of rows for analytics, so bytes per second and cost per byte matter; nobody waits on a single event in milliseconds.

title: Five stacked layers: from engines down to tape
body: A lake is easiest to reason about as a stack. At the top are compute engines such as Spark, Trino, Flink and BigQuery. Below them sits the table format and catalog: Hive, Iceberg, Hudi or Delta. Next is the file format: Parquet, ORC or Google's Capacitor. Then the storage layer: HDFS, S3, GCS, Tectonic or Colossus. At the bottom is the physical media: HDD, flash or tape. Keeping these layers separate in your head avoids confusing their jobs.
deeper:
The chapter describes three core lake layers, the storage layer, the file format and the table format, with engines above and media below. Each has a distinct responsibility. The storage layer stores bytes and names, meaning paths or object keys; it does not know what a table is. The file format decides how rows and columns are laid out inside each file, for example grouping values by column. The table format tracks which files make up a table at each point in time, which gives transactions and snapshots.

The separation matters when things change. Uber swapped its storage layer from HDFS to Google Cloud Storage while keeping the layers above untouched. Netflix created Iceberg, a table-format layer, because the storage layer below it, S3, could not provide atomic renames that Hive depended on. Colossus does tiering at the media level, invisible to everything above. When diagnosing a lake problem, asking which layer owns it quickly narrows the fix: small files are a storage and table-maintenance issue, while slow commits on S3 are a table-format issue.

quiz.q: Which lake layer is responsible for knowing which files make up a table at a given time?
quiz.a: The table format (Iceberg, Hudi, Delta). The storage layer only knows bytes and names; the file format only lays out data inside each file.

title: HDFS: one NameNode holds the tree, DataNodes hold 3 copies
body: From about 2008 to 2020, most big data lakes ran on HDFS, the Hadoop Distributed File System. HDFS keeps all file metadata in a single NameNode, a server that holds the entire directory tree in memory. The actual data blocks live on many DataNodes. By default, each block is copied 3 times across DataNodes for durability. This simple design powered the first generation of large lakes before its scaling limits became painful.
deeper:
HDFS had real strengths. The first was data locality: the scheduler could run a task on the very machine holding the block it needed, so reads skipped the network entirely. In an era of slower, oversubscribed datacenter networks this was a big deal. The second was cost: it was open source and ran on cheap commodity disks.

But the architecture baked in three problems that grew with scale. The single NameNode keeps every file and block in RAM, so metadata size is bounded by one machine's memory. Triple replication means every petabyte of data needs three petabytes of disk. And because DataNodes double as compute nodes, storage and compute are tied together. Each of these problems pushed companies toward the second generation of lakes on object storage, or toward custom systems like Meta's Tectonic. Understanding the HDFS design is therefore the baseline for understanding why modern lakes look the way they do.

quiz.q: What was data locality in HDFS, and why was it valuable?
quiz.a: Running a task on the machine that holds the block it reads, so the read skips the network, which mattered when networks were slower.

title: The NameNode RAM ceiling: every file costs memory
body: HDFS's first scaling problem is the NameNode. Every file and every block is tracked in the NameNode's RAM. More files means more memory, which in turn means longer garbage-collection pauses and more lock contention on that single server. Because one machine holds the whole namespace, the total number of files a cluster can hold is capped by that machine. As lakes grew into billions of files, this became a hard limit.
deeper:
Uber offers a public example. In 2018 Uber wrote that its HDFS data grew more than 400% in 2017. By late 2016, NameNode queue time had passed 500 ms, against a normal level of under 10 ms, so every metadata operation across the cluster was slowed.

Uber's fixes show the typical toolbox. ViewFs placed several physical namespaces behind one virtual view, effectively splitting the metadata load across multiple NameNodes while users saw one tree. They also did upgrades, tuned garbage collection, and built small-file merge tools, because reducing the file count directly relieves NameNode memory.

The lesson is that the NameNode problem is really a file-count problem, not a byte-count problem. A cluster can hold petabytes comfortably in large files and still fall over under millions of tiny ones. This is why the small-files problem is so tightly linked to HDFS, and why moving to object stores, which have no single metadata server, was attractive.

quiz.q: Why does file count rather than total bytes drive NameNode trouble?
quiz.a: Every file and block occupies NameNode RAM, so millions of small files exhaust memory and cause GC pauses and lock contention even when total bytes are modest.

title: 3x replication vs RS(6,3): 200% overhead down to 50%
body: HDFS's second problem is cost. By default every block is stored three times, so every petabyte of data needs three petabytes of disk, a 200% overhead. HDFS 3 added erasure coding, with RS(6,3) as the default policy: data is split into 6 chunks plus 3 parity chunks, cutting overhead to about 50%. But erasure-coded files lose some features, such as append, and most reads go across racks.
deeper:
Reed-Solomon RS(6,3) stores 6 data chunks and 3 parity chunks, so 9 chunks hold 6 chunks' worth of data. Any 6 of the 9 are enough to rebuild the original, so it survives the loss of 3 chunks while using 1.5x raw capacity instead of 3x. At lake scale, going from 3 PB to 1.5 PB per petabyte stored is an enormous saving.

The trade-offs are why replication did not disappear. Erasure-coded files in HDFS cannot be appended to, which clashes with workloads that grow files over time. Reads usually cross racks because the chunks are spread out, so data locality is weakened. Rebuilding a lost chunk also requires reading several others. The pattern repeats across systems in this chapter: Meta's Tectonic uses RS(9,6) for long-lived warehouse data and RS(3,3) for short-lived shuffle output, and Meta moved warm photos from 3.6x to 2.1x effective replication. More aggressive coding fits colder, more stable data.

quiz.q: What does HDFS give up when it switches a file from 3x replication to RS(6,3) erasure coding?
quiz.a: Features like append, plus locality: most reads go across racks. In exchange overhead drops from 200% to about 50%.

title: When DataNodes are compute nodes, disk forces CPU purchases
body: HDFS's third problem is that storage and compute are tied together. A DataNode is also a compute node, because data locality depends on running tasks where the blocks live. So if a team needs more disk but not more CPU, it still has to buy whole servers with both. Over time, data volume and compute demand grow at different rates, and the coupled design wastes money on whichever resource is not the bottleneck.
deeper:
This coupling was a deliberate choice, not an accident. Data locality, HDFS's big advantage, only works if the machine storing a block can also run the task that reads it. The price is that the cluster's shape is fixed: disk and CPU come in the ratio of the server model you buy.

Lake data tends to grow relentlessly, because event logs are append-only and retention periods are long, while compute needs fluctuate with analysts' and jobs' demand. A coupled cluster must be sized for the larger of the two, leaving the other idle. Separating them lets storage be built from dense disk-heavy machines or rented from an object store, while compute runs on clusters sized to the current workload and shut down when idle.

This is the third of the reasons companies moved lakes from HDFS to object storage around 2015 to 2020, alongside the NameNode limit and the cost of triple replication. Meta's Tectonic addressed a related problem inside its own fleet.

quiz.q: Why did HDFS tie storage and compute together in the first place?
quiz.a: Data locality required tasks to run on the machine holding the block, so DataNodes doubled as compute nodes, fixing the disk-to-CPU ratio.

title: Uber 2016-2018: HDFS grew 400% and the NameNode choked
body: Uber wrote in 2018 that its HDFS data grew more than 400% in 2017. In late 2016, NameNode queue time passed 500 ms, compared with a normal level of under 10 ms, meaning every metadata operation across the cluster was dramatically slowed. Uber's fixes included ViewFs (several physical namespaces behind one virtual view), software upgrades, garbage-collection tuning and tools to merge small files. It is a textbook case of first-generation lake scaling pain.
deeper:
Each fix targets a different part of the NameNode problem. ViewFs attacks the single-namespace limit: instead of one NameNode holding everything, several physical namespaces each hold a part, while users and jobs see one virtual tree. Upgrades bring performance fixes in newer HDFS releases. Garbage-collection tuning reduces the pauses that a huge in-memory heap causes on the Java-based NameNode. Small-file merge tools reduce the number of objects the NameNode must track at all, often the most direct lever.

A jump from under 10 ms to over 500 ms is a 50-fold slowdown in metadata operations, which affects every job listing directories, opening files or creating output. Uber's growth was driven by business expansion and data-hungry analytics, which is typical. This experience fed later decisions. Uber built Hudi on HDFS to handle mutable data, and in 2024 announced a move of its batch analytics and ML storage from on-premises Hadoop to Google Cloud Storage.

quiz.q: How does merging small files help an overloaded HDFS NameNode?
quiz.a: The NameNode keeps every file and block in RAM; fewer, larger files mean less memory, shorter GC pauses and less lock contention.

title: The small-files problem: lakes want 1 GB, streams make 7 MB
body: The small-files problem is the most common pain in any data lake. Lakes work best with files of 128 MB to 1 GB. But streaming jobs flush a file every few minutes per partition, and every parallel task writes its own output file. The result is millions of files of only a few KB or MB each. The data volume is fine; the sheer number of files is what overwhelms metadata systems, request budgets and query planners.
deeper:
Small files are a natural side effect of how data arrives, not a mistake. Freshness pushes streaming jobs to flush often, and parallelism means each task writes separately, so a job with hundreds of partitions and frequent flushes multiplies file counts quickly.

The problem is described as permanent in the chapter's takeaways: you cannot design it away, only manage it continuously. That is why the standard answer, compaction, is treated as an ongoing platform service rather than a one-time cleanup.

It also hurts across generations. On HDFS the cost lands on NameNode memory. On object stores, which have no single metadata server, the cost shifts to per-request latency and fees, because every file needs its own LIST entry and GET. Both designs also suffer at the file-format level, since tiny Parquet files have tiny column chunks. Moving from HDFS to S3 therefore changes who pays for small files but does not make the problem go away.

quiz.q: Why does the small-files problem hurt both HDFS and object-store lakes despite their different metadata designs?
quiz.a: HDFS pays per file in NameNode RAM; object stores pay per file in LIST/GET requests, latency and fees. Both lose compression and planning speed.

title: Three ways tiny files hurt: metadata, requests, compression
body: Small files hurt in three ways. Metadata cost: on HDFS each file consumes NameNode memory, and on object stores each file needs its own LIST entry and GET. Request cost and latency: 1 GB stored as 10,000 files of 100 KB takes 10,000 requests, each with fixed latency of often tens of ms and, on S3, a price. Worse compression and planning: tiny files have tiny column chunks, so Parquet compresses poorly, and planners must open every file's footer.
deeper:
The request math is the easiest to feel. Reading 1 GB as one file is essentially one long sequential stream. Reading it as 10,000 files of 100 KB means 10,000 separate round trips, each paying fixed setup latency, often tens of milliseconds, before any bytes move. Even with parallelism, that overhead dominates, and on S3 every GET is billed.

The compression effect is subtler. Columnar formats get their efficiency from long runs of similar values within a column chunk. A file holding only a few thousand rows produces short chunks, so encodings like dictionary and run-length have less to work with, and per-file headers and footers become a larger share of total bytes.

Planning cost adds up too. Before running a query, an engine reads each Parquet file's footer to learn its schema and column statistics. With millions of files, planning alone can take longer than the scan. Each of these costs scales with file count, which is why fixing file count via compaction improves all three at once.

quiz.q: Why do tiny Parquet files compress worse than large ones?
quiz.a: Each file has only short column chunks, so encodings like run-length and dictionary find fewer repeats, and fixed per-file overhead is a larger fraction.

title: Back-of-envelope: 52 million files a year from one table
body: Take a table receiving 1 TB per day from a streaming job with 500 partitions that flushes every 5 minutes. That is 500 x 288 = 144,000 files per day, averaging about 7 MB each. After one year the table holds about 52 million files. If the same data were stored as 512 MB files, it would be about 2,000 files per day, or 730,000 per year: 70 times fewer objects to list, open and track.
deeper:
The arithmetic is worth internalizing because it shows how innocent settings multiply. A 5-minute flush interval gives 288 flushes per day (1,440 minutes divided by 5). Multiply by 500 partitions and you get 144,000 files daily. Divide 1 TB by 144,000 and each file is only about 7 MB, well below the 128 MB to 1 GB sweet spot.

Over 365 days, 144,000 files per day becomes roughly 52 million files for one table. On HDFS every one of those sits in NameNode memory; on an object store every query planning pass may need to list and open a large share of them.

The same terabyte per day in 512 MB files is about 2,000 files, or 730,000 a year. Nothing about the data changed, only the file layout. This is why the usual design keeps small, frequent files for freshness during the current hour or day, then compacts each partition into large files once it closes. Reducing partitions or flush frequency is the other lever, at the cost of freshness.

quiz.q: In the example, which two settings multiply to produce 144,000 files per day, and what are the levers to reduce it?
quiz.a: 500 partitions times 288 five-minute flushes. Reduce partitions or flush frequency (hurting freshness), or compact closed partitions into large files.

title: Compaction: rewrite many small files as few big ones
body: Compaction is the fix for small files. It is a background job that reads many small files and rewrites them as fewer, larger files. It then updates the table metadata so readers switch to the new files atomically, meaning a query sees either all old files or all new ones, never a mix. The old files are deleted later, after readers that might still use them have finished. File count drops, and queries get faster.
deeper:
The atomic switch is what makes compaction safe on a live table. Readers that started before the switch keep seeing the old files, while new readers see the compacted ones. This is exactly the kind of guarantee table formats such as Iceberg and Hudi provide, by recording which files make up the table at each snapshot. Deleting old files later, rather than immediately, avoids breaking queries still in flight.

Compaction is not free. It reads and writes the data again, which is write amplification: compact the same data three times and you have written it four times. It competes with production jobs for cluster capacity. It can also conflict with writers on the same partition, forcing retries.

The usual design balances these: write small files quickly for freshness, then compact a partition once it is closed, for example once the hour has passed. Closed partitions no longer receive writes, so conflicts disappear, and the data is compacted once rather than repeatedly.

quiz.q: Why do lakes usually compact a partition only after it is closed, such as once the hour has passed?
quiz.a: No more writers touch it, so compaction avoids conflicts and retries, and data is rewritten once instead of repeatedly, limiting write amplification.

title: LinkedIn OpenHouse: table maintenance as a platform service
body: LinkedIn built OpenHouse, a control plane for lakehouse tables, in production since late 2022. It stores Iceberg tables on HDFS and runs table maintenance as scheduled Spark jobs: snapshot expiration, orphan file deletion, manifest compaction, retention (data purging and partition expiration), and cross-datacenter snapshot replication. The lesson: at scale, compaction and cleanup are not something each team should remember to do. They must be a platform service that runs automatically for every table.
deeper:
Each maintenance task addresses a specific way lake tables decay. Snapshot expiration removes old table versions that table formats keep for time travel, which would otherwise pin old files forever. Orphan file deletion removes files written by failed jobs that no snapshot references. Manifest compaction shrinks the metadata files Iceberg uses to track data files, so planning stays fast. Retention purges data and expires partitions past their allowed age. Cross-datacenter snapshot replication keeps copies in other sites.

If each team must schedule these itself, some teams forget, some do it wrong, and costs creep up invisibly. By centralizing maintenance in a control plane, LinkedIn makes every table get the same hygiene by default.

OpenHouse reappears later in the chapter for retention: because data copies spread through derived tables and training sets, building retention into the table platform itself helps ensure deletion policies are actually enforced. LinkedIn's approach keeps its large owned HDFS fleet while adding central table governance on top.

quiz.q: Why is it risky to leave compaction and cleanup to each individual team?
quiz.a: Teams forget or do it inconsistently, so small files, old snapshots, orphans and over-retained data pile up; a central platform applies maintenance uniformly.

title: Why lakes moved from HDFS to S3, GCS and Azure Blob
body: Around 2015 to 2020, many companies moved their lakes from HDFS to object storage such as S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob or an internal equivalent. The reasons mirror HDFS's problems. Object stores have no single NameNode, so the file-count limit goes away, though per-request cost remains. The provider runs erasure coding and replication, so there is no 3x HDFS copy to manage. And storage and compute scale independently, so compute clusters can be ephemeral.
deeper:
Each benefit maps to one HDFS pain. The NameNode memory ceiling disappears because object-store metadata is distributed and managed by the provider. The expense of triple replication is handled inside the provider, which applies its own erasure coding and replication and bills per GB-month. The coupling of disk and CPU ends because storage is a separate service; compute can be rented for a job and released afterward.

The cost model changes too: instead of buying servers, you pay per GB-month plus per request. That makes request counts, and therefore file counts, a direct line item on the bill, which is why small files stay painful.

The move was not free. Every read now crosses the network, there is no data locality, and object stores lack atomic directory renames. Those gaps are why table formats like Iceberg and Hudi became essential in the second generation. Netflix, Uber and others each show a different path through this transition, and Meta shows an alternative: building its own exabyte-scale system instead.

quiz.q: Moving to an object store removes the NameNode limit. Which small-file cost remains?
quiz.a: Per-request cost: every file still needs its own LIST entry and GET, each with latency and, on clouds like S3, a fee.

title: No data locality: every read crosses the network, and it's fine
body: Object-store lakes give up data locality: compute no longer runs on the machine holding the data, so every read goes over the network. This works for two reasons. Datacenter networks became fast and flat, so reaching any storage server is cheap. And columnar formats such as Parquet read only the columns a query needs, reducing bytes on the wire. Together these made remote reads acceptable for analytics, enabling the separation of storage and compute.
deeper:
Data locality was HDFS's headline advantage in its era, when networks were slower and oversubscribed, so pulling data across racks was a real bottleneck. As networks improved, the gap between reading a local disk and reading over the network narrowed enough that flexibility became worth more than locality.

Columnar formats amplify the effect. If a query touches 5 of 100 columns, it pulls only those column chunks, so the network carries a small fraction of the table. Combined with high aggregate bandwidth from many storage servers, this keeps scans fast.

The trade-off shows up in the comparison table: HDFS lakes offer data locality, while object-store lakes read everything over the network. In exchange, object-store lakes make scaling compute separately easy rather than hard. Note that erasure-coded HDFS already gave up much of its locality, since most reads of RS(6,3) data cross racks. The industry trend is clear: locality mattered less once networks and file formats caught up.

quiz.q: What two developments made giving up data locality acceptable for object-store lakes?
quiz.a: Fast, flat datacenter networks made remote reads cheap, and columnar formats read only needed columns, cutting bytes sent over the network.

title: Object stores can't rename a directory atomically
body: Object stores have different semantics from a file system. There are no real directories, only keys that look like paths, so renaming a directory is not atomic: it means copying and deleting many objects one by one. Old Hive-style tables committed a job by renaming a temporary directory into place, which is slow and unsafe on an object store. Table formats like Iceberg solve this by tracking files in metadata instead of relying on directory listings.
deeper:
On HDFS, renaming a directory is a single metadata operation on the NameNode, so it happens all at once. That made it a convenient commit mechanism: a job writes its output to a temporary directory, then renames it to the final location, and readers see either nothing or the complete result.

On an object store, a directory is just a shared key prefix. Renaming it means copying every object to a new key and deleting the old, which takes time proportional to the number of files and can fail halfway. Readers might see partial output, and listing a prefix to find a table's files is itself slow when there are many.

Iceberg's answer is to stop treating the directory as the source of truth. A table's metadata explicitly lists its data files for each snapshot, and a commit atomically swaps a pointer to a new metadata version. The comparison table summarizes: HDFS has atomic rename, object-store lakes do not and need a table format. This gap is one main reason Iceberg was created.

quiz.q: Why was the Hive commit-by-rename pattern unsafe on an object store?
quiz.a: Directories are just key prefixes, so renaming means copying and deleting objects one by one: slow, non-atomic, and readers can see partial results.

title: HDFS lake vs object-store lake at a glance
body: Comparing the two generations side by side: HDFS keeps metadata in one NameNode (or a federation) in RAM, while object stores distribute metadata managed by the provider. HDFS uses 3x replicas or RS(6,3); object stores use provider-managed erasure coding and replication. HDFS offers data locality and atomic rename; object stores offer neither, needing a table format for commits. Scaling compute separately is hard on HDFS, easy on object stores. HDFS means buying servers; object stores charge per GB-month plus requests.
deeper:
Reading the table as a set of trades clarifies when each generation fits. HDFS wins on locality and file-system semantics like atomic rename, but concentrates risk and limits in the NameNode, and couples storage to compute. Object stores win on elastic scale and operational simplicity, with the provider handling redundancy, but give up locality and need extra machinery, a table format, to provide safe commits.

The cost model row is easy to overlook but important. Buying servers is a capital expense sized in advance; paying per GB-month plus requests is an operating expense that tracks usage. With per-request billing, file counts and access patterns appear directly on the monthly bill, which makes the small-files problem and tiering decisions financial concerns, not just performance ones.

Many companies ended up somewhere in between. LinkedIn stays on HDFS but adds Iceberg through OpenHouse. Uber is moving to Google Cloud Storage while keeping the HDFS API. Meta built its own system, Tectonic, rather than choosing either.

quiz.q: How does the cost model of an object-store lake change the importance of file counts compared with HDFS?
quiz.a: Object stores bill per request as well as per GB-month, so every extra file adds LIST and GET charges directly to the bill.

section: 7.3.1 Netflix: the S3 lake and the birth of Iceberg
title: Netflix built Iceberg because Hive on S3 was slow and unsafe
body: Netflix runs its data warehouse on Amazon S3, with compute clusters kept separate. Its engineers created Iceberg, later donated to Apache, because Hive tables on S3 had two problems. They were slow to plan, since finding a table's files meant listing directories. And they were unsafe to change, since there was no atomic commit. The storage lesson: on an object store, the table format must take over the file system's old job of knowing which files belong to a table.
deeper:
Netflix is the cloud-first example in the chapter's comparison: Amazon S3 for storage, Iceberg (created at Netflix) with Parquet for the table and file layers, chosen because the company runs in the cloud with separate compute.

The two Hive problems map directly to object-store semantics. Slow planning came from directory listings: to find a partition's files, Hive listed a prefix, and listing is slow and paginated on S3 when there are many objects. Unsafe changes came from the lack of atomic rename, so a commit could leave readers seeing partial output.

Iceberg fixes both by keeping an explicit, versioned list of data files in table metadata. Planning reads that metadata rather than listing directories, and a commit swaps to a new metadata version atomically. The broader principle outlives the specific tool: when you move from a file system to an object store, some responsibilities the file system quietly handled, such as consistent membership and atomic changes, must move up into a higher layer.

quiz.q: What job did the file system used to do that Iceberg takes over on an object store?
quiz.a: Knowing which files belong to a table, with atomic changes, tracked in versioned metadata instead of directory listings and renames.

section: 7.3.2 Uber: from HDFS with Hudi to Google Cloud Storage
title: Uber's Hudi: updating immutable HDFS files within minutes
body: Uber built Hudi (Hadoop Upserts Deletes and Incrementals) and described it publicly in March 2017. The problem: HDFS files are immutable, but Uber's trip data changes, for example a trip gets a rating or a fare is corrected. Rewriting whole partitions for each change was too slow. Hudi keeps metadata about commit times and file versions, so it can apply updates to HDFS data within minutes and let downstream jobs pull only changes since a given time.
deeper:
Hudi addresses a mismatch between storage and data. A lake file system is built for append-only, write-once data, but business records like trips are mutable. Without Hudi, correcting a single fare might mean rewriting an entire day's partition, which is expensive and delays freshness.

By tracking commit times and file versions in metadata, Hudi can write new versions of only the affected files and record which version is current. That gives upserts (update or insert) and deletes on top of immutable storage.

The incremental part is equally valuable. Because every change is tagged with a commit time, downstream jobs can ask for only records that changed since their last run instead of rescanning whole tables. That cuts compute and speeds pipelines. Uber later donated Hudi to Apache. In the chapter's comparison, Uber's choice of Hudi with Parquet is explained by mutable trip data. Like Iceberg at Netflix, Hudi is an example of a table format created to fix a gap in the storage layer beneath it.

quiz.q: What problem with HDFS did Hudi solve for Uber's trip data?
quiz.a: HDFS files are immutable but trip data changes; Hudi tracks commits and file versions to apply updates within minutes without rewriting whole partitions.

section: 7.3.2 Uber: from HDFS with Hudi to Google Cloud Storage
title: Uber 2024: moving an exabyte Hadoop lake to Google Cloud
body: On May 30, 2024, Uber published its plan to move batch analytics and ML training from on-premises Hadoop to Google Cloud Platform. Uber described its installation as one of the largest Hadoop deployments in the world: more than 1 exabyte of data across tens of thousands of servers in each of its two regions. The first phase uses Google Cloud Storage as the lake's storage and moves the rest of the stack to cloud VMs.
deeper:
The mechanism that makes the first phase possible is a cloud storage connector that implements the Hadoop FileSystem interface. Existing jobs call the same HDFS API as before, and the connector translates those calls to Google Cloud Storage. Jobs therefore run without code changes, even though the bytes now live in a completely different system.

The rest of the stack moves to cloud virtual machines as infrastructure as a service (IaaS), which again keeps the software largely the same. Only in later phases would Uber adopt managed services such as Dataproc and BigQuery, which would require more changes to how jobs run.

In the chapter's comparison, Uber's motivation is described as leaving behind mutable-data problems first (via Hudi), then exiting data-center capital expense. Uber's history spans both lake generations: an HDFS lake that hit NameNode limits in 2016 to 2018, Hudi in 2017 to manage mutable data, and in 2024 a shift to an object store. It is a rare public account of migrating exabyte-scale storage.

quiz.q: How did Uber make existing Hadoop jobs run unchanged on Google Cloud Storage?
quiz.a: A cloud storage connector implements the Hadoop FileSystem interface, so jobs keep calling the HDFS API while bytes are stored in GCS.

section: 7.3.2 Uber: from HDFS with Hudi to Google Cloud Storage
title: Senior lens: keep the narrowest interface stable, move the bytes
body: Notice the order Uber chose for its cloud migration. It swapped the storage layer first, behind the same HDFS API, and left the jobs alone. This is the classic low-risk migration pattern: keep the interface, change the implementation, then modernize the layers above later. When you plan a lake migration, ask one question: what is the narrowest interface I can keep stable while I move the bytes? That interface becomes your safety boundary.
deeper:
The value of this order is diagnostic as much as practical. If you change storage and rewrite jobs at the same time and something breaks, you cannot tell which change caused it. Changing one layer at a time means any failure points to the storage layer, not to a rewritten job, and jobs do not all need to be touched or retested at once.

The narrow interface here is the Hadoop FileSystem API. Everything above it, thousands of jobs, stays the same; everything below it, the bytes, moves. Choosing the narrowest stable interface minimizes the surface area that must behave identically in old and new worlds.

The same idea shows up elsewhere in the chapter. Meta's Tectonic replaced HDFS for the warehouse, and the layered view of a lake, with separate storage, file format and table format layers, is exactly what makes such swaps possible. Modernizing the upper layers, such as adopting BigQuery or Dataproc, becomes a later, separate project once the bytes are safely in place.

quiz.q: Uber moved storage to GCS first and kept Hadoop jobs unchanged. What risk does this order reduce?
quiz.a: It changes one layer at a time, so failures point to storage, not rewritten jobs, and jobs needn't all be touched or retested at once.

title: Meta's HDFS era: tens of clusters and a bin-packing puzzle
body: Meta did not move to a public cloud. Instead it built its own exabyte-scale file system, Tectonic, described at FAST 2021. Before Tectonic, Meta's data warehouse ran on HDFS. HDFS clusters had size limits, so Meta needed tens of HDFS clusters per datacenter and had to split datasets across them. The Tectonic paper calls this a two-dimensional bin-packing problem: fitting both storage capacity and read throughput into each cluster at once.
deeper:
Bin packing means placing items into containers without exceeding their limits. Here it is two-dimensional because each dataset needs both space and IO throughput. A dataset might fit a cluster's free capacity but overload its disks' throughput, or vice versa. Operators had to juggle datasets across many clusters to balance both, and any cluster's leftover capacity in one dimension was often stranded because nothing fit the other.

This is the NameNode ceiling showing up operationally. Because each HDFS cluster is limited in size, a large warehouse must be split across many clusters, and splitting creates the packing problem, plus the overhead of running many independent systems.

Meta's choice to build rather than buy fits its scale and ownership of its fleet. Its answer was a single file system large enough to host the warehouse as one tenant among others, removing the need to split datasets. In the chapter's comparison, Meta's reasons are exabyte scale and consolidating clusters, with ORC-based warehouse formats as its file layer.

quiz.q: Why did Meta's HDFS warehouse face a two-dimensional bin-packing problem?
quiz.a: HDFS cluster size limits forced datasets across tens of clusters, and each placement had to fit both capacity and throughput limits simultaneously.

title: Tectonic: 10x fewer warehouse clusters, 10.7 billion files
body: Tectonic replaced three Meta systems: HDFS, Haystack and f4. Moving the warehouse to Tectonic cut the number of warehouse clusters by 10 times. One multitenant production cluster described in the paper had 1,590 PB of capacity, 1,250 PB used, 10.7 billion files and 4,208 storage nodes. Long-lived warehouse data is typically encoded with RS(9,6), while short-lived data like map-reduce shuffle output uses RS(3,3), matching redundancy to how long data lives.
deeper:
The numbers show what escaping the NameNode ceiling buys. 10.7 billion files in one cluster would be unthinkable for a single in-memory HDFS NameNode, and consolidating means fewer systems to run and no more splitting datasets across clusters.

The encoding choices illustrate matching redundancy to data lifetime. RS(9,6) means 9 data chunks plus 6 parity chunks: 15 chunks for 9 chunks of data, about 1.67x raw space, while tolerating the loss of 6 chunks. That strong protection suits data kept for a long time. RS(3,3) is 3 data plus 3 parity, 2x space, but with only 6 chunks per stripe, writing and reading are simpler and faster, which suits short-lived shuffle output that will be deleted soon.

Tectonic replacing Haystack and f4, Meta's hot and warm blob stores, is also notable. It means the separate tiered systems described in the f4 paper were eventually folded into one multitenant file system, with differences expressed through encoding and placement rather than separate storage products.

quiz.q: Why would Meta use RS(3,3) for shuffle output but RS(9,6) for long-lived warehouse data?
quiz.a: Short-lived shuffle data favors simpler, faster coding with fewer chunks; long-lived data needs stronger durability at lower space overhead, which RS(9,6) gives.

title: Multitenancy lets the warehouse borrow idle disk IO
body: Tectonic shows a benefit of multitenancy, where several very different workloads share one storage system. Meta's warehouse and its blob storage (photos, videos and similar objects) ran as tenants on the same Tectonic clusters. During traffic spikes, the warehouse could use spare disk IO from the blob-storage tenant. Separate clusters would leave that idle IO stranded, while a shared system lets one tenant absorb another's unused capacity.
deeper:
Each workload has its own rhythm. Warehouse jobs are bursty, with heavy scans at certain times, while blob storage has different peaks. If each runs on its own dedicated cluster, each must be provisioned for its own peak, and the gap between peak and average is wasted.

Pooling resources in one system smooths this out. When the warehouse spikes, it can draw on IO that the blob tenant is not using at that moment. This is the same economic logic as consolidating many HDFS clusters into fewer Tectonic clusters: bigger pools waste less stranded capacity, whether that capacity is disk space or disk throughput.

It also ties back to the two-dimensional bin-packing problem Meta faced on HDFS. When clusters are small and isolated, leftover throughput in one cannot help another. In a large shared cluster, throughput becomes a fungible, shared resource. Google's Colossus reflects a similar goal, trying to keep disks both full and busy by placing hot and cold data together across its fleet.

quiz.q: How did multitenancy on Tectonic help Meta's warehouse during traffic spikes?
quiz.a: The warehouse shared clusters with blob storage and could use the blob tenant's spare disk IO, instead of that throughput sitting idle in a separate cluster.

title: BigQuery's Capacitor reorders rows to compress better
body: BigQuery is a fully managed warehouse: users never see files. Underneath, tables are stored in Capacitor, Google's internal columnar format, on Colossus, Google's cluster file system. Google described Capacitor in 2016. Beyond standard encodings like run-length and dictionary, a notable idea is row reordering. Finding the best row order for compression is NP-complete, so Capacitor uses a heuristic based on data types and query patterns to make run-length encoding work better.
deeper:
Run-length encoding stores a repeated value once along with how many times it repeats, so it shines when identical values sit next to each other. Row order therefore changes compression: sort a table so similar rows cluster together and runs get longer. Because rows are shared across all columns, the order that best helps one column may hurt another, and searching for the optimal order is NP-complete, meaning no known efficient exact algorithm exists at scale. Capacitor settles for a good heuristic guided by column types and how the table is queried.

Colossus provides the durability and security underneath: encryption at rest, Reed-Solomon coding and geo-replication. BigQuery also re-optimizes storage in the background, which is like automatic compaction and layout tuning that users never have to schedule.

In the comparison table, Google's reason is being fully managed, with storage fully hidden. That contrasts with open lakes, where teams like LinkedIn's must build platforms such as OpenHouse to run maintenance themselves.

quiz.q: Why does row order affect how well Capacitor compresses a table?
quiz.a: Run-length encoding compresses runs of identical values; reordering rows groups similar values together, lengthening runs. The optimal order is NP-complete, so a heuristic is used.

title: Colossus quietly moves data from flash to disk as it ages
body: Colossus also places data by temperature. Google wrote in 2021 that hot data goes on flash and data moves to larger-capacity disks as it ages, while trying to keep disks both full and busy. This is tiering inside the file system, invisible to the user. Applications and BigQuery users never pick a storage class; the system decides where bytes should live based on how actively they are used.
deeper:
The goal of keeping disks both full and busy captures the core tension of tiering. Large-capacity disks are cheap per byte but can serve only limited IOPS. Fill them only with cold data and they sit idle; fill them with hot data and they cannot keep up. Mixing temperatures sensibly uses both capacity and throughput, while flash absorbs the hottest reads.

This is the first of the two ways to tier that the chapter later describes: transparent tiering inside the storage system, as opposed to tiering exposed to customers as storage classes with different prices. With transparent tiering, the operator owns the decision and has direct visibility into access rates, so it can move data by actual IOPS per TB rather than guesses.

Meta's f4 is another example of internal tiering, moving warm photos to a system with lower replication overhead. The chapter's comparison table lists internal tiering as moving by access and IOPS per TB, with retrieval fees not applicable, since it operates within the provider's own fleet.

quiz.q: Why does Colossus try to keep disks 'both full and busy' when placing data by temperature?
quiz.a: Big disks are cheap per byte but IOPS-limited; mixing temperatures uses both capacity and throughput instead of leaving disks idle or overloaded.

title: Five lakes compared: Netflix, Uber, LinkedIn, Meta, Google
body: Five companies, five choices. Netflix: Amazon S3 with Iceberg (created there) and Parquet, as a cloud-first company with separate compute. Uber: HDFS moving to GCS (announced 2024), with Hudi and Parquet, driven by mutable trip data and exiting data-center capital expense. LinkedIn: HDFS with Iceberg via OpenHouse, reflecting a large owned fleet and central table governance. Meta: Tectonic replacing HDFS, ORC-based formats, for exabyte scale and cluster consolidation. Google: Colossus with Capacitor in fully managed BigQuery.
deeper:
The comparison shows there is no single right lake. Each choice follows from the company's situation.

Netflix was born in the cloud, so S3 was the natural storage layer, and the gaps in object-store semantics led it to invent Iceberg. Uber's data changes after it is written, so it needed Hudi for upserts on immutable HDFS; later, the cost of owning data centers pushed it toward GCS. LinkedIn owns a large fleet and chose to modernize the table layer, adding Iceberg governance with OpenHouse rather than migrating storage. Meta operates at exabyte scale and built Tectonic to collapse many HDFS clusters into far fewer. Google hides storage entirely behind BigQuery, pairing its own columnar format with its own file system.

The pattern across all five is the layered model: companies change the layer that hurts most. Sometimes that is the table format (Netflix, LinkedIn), sometimes storage (Uber, Meta), and sometimes the whole stack is vertically integrated (Google).

quiz.q: LinkedIn and Uber both started on HDFS. How did their modernization strategies differ?
quiz.a: LinkedIn kept HDFS and added Iceberg governance via OpenHouse; Uber added Hudi for mutable data, then began moving storage itself to Google Cloud Storage.

title: Meta's f4 data: day-old content gets 100x more requests
body: The best public evidence that data cools comes from Meta's f4 paper, OSDI 2014. It studied nine types of user BLOBs (Binary Large OBjects, such as photos, videos and attachments) using a two-week trace. For all nine types, content less than one day old received more than 100 times the request rate of one-year-old content. For eight of nine types, request rate dropped 10 times in under a week. For six types, it dropped 100 times within 60 days.
deeper:
These numbers show both how extreme and how fast cooling is. A 100-fold gap between a new object and a year-old one means treating them the same, on the same media and redundancy, wastes money on the old one or starves the new one.

The speed matters as much as the magnitude. A 10-fold drop within a week for eight of nine types means most of an object's lifetime demand happens almost immediately after upload. That is intuitive for social media: people view a new photo when it is posted, then rarely again.

The chapter calls this the core fact of storage economics: most data is cold, and it gets cold fast. A small hot part needs fast media; a large cold part needs cheap media. The lifecycle can be pictured as a sequence: a new photo is uploaded; it is hot, with many reads in the first day; reads drop about 10 times within a week; it becomes warm after about one to three months; then cold, rarely read but kept for years; and finally archived or deleted by retention policy.

quiz.q: What does the f4 trace imply about putting new and year-old BLOBs on the same storage?
quiz.a: Demand differs by over 100x, so uniform storage either overspends on cold data or underserves hot data; each needs different media.

title: Hot-to-warm cutoffs: one month, three for photos, never for avatars
body: Meta's f4 paper derived safe cutoffs for moving BLOBs from hot to warm storage. For most types, one month was safe. Ordinary photos used three months. Profile photos were never moved to warm storage, because they stay popular long after upload. The paper also found warm objects dominate: more than 80% of objects in the oldest interval studied, and more than 89% in the newest, were warm across all types. Most stored data is warm or colder.
deeper:
The cutoff is set per type, not globally, and that is the practical lesson. Different content cools at different speeds. Profile photos are displayed next to a user's activity everywhere, so they keep getting requests for about a year or more and keep too many requests per TB for warm storage. Ordinary photos cool more slowly than attachments or other content, hence their longer three-month window.

The one-month cutoff for most types came with a safety margin. Near-worst-case load dropped below warm-tier capacity within about a week, and delete rates also fall with age, so waiting a month meant objects were solidly cold and unlikely to be deleted soon after moving.

The 80% to 89% figures explain why warm storage matters so much financially. If most objects are warm, then the redundancy overhead of warm storage, not hot storage, dominates total cost. That is why Meta invested in f4, which cut effective replication from Haystack's 3.6x to 2.8x and later 2.1x.

quiz.q: What evidence from the f4 paper supports a one-month hot-to-warm cutoff, and why were profile photos never moved?
quiz.a: Near-worst-case load fell below warm capacity (20 IOPS/TB) within a week and deletes decline with age, giving margin. Profile photos stayed popular about a year.

title: Warm storage is sized in IOPS per TB, about 20 for f4
body: The hardware link behind tiering is IOPS, input/output operations per second. In f4, 4 TB disks delivered about 80 IOPS at acceptable latency. Divide 80 by 4 and each terabyte stored can serve about 20 IOPS, so warm storage was sized for about 20 IOPS per TB. Data can move to dense storage only once its request rate per TB falls below that level; otherwise the disks cannot keep up with reads.
deeper:
This turns tiering from a vague idea into arithmetic. A disk has a roughly fixed number of IOPS regardless of capacity. As disks get denser, the IOPS available per stored terabyte falls. A dense warm tier is cheap per byte precisely because it packs many bytes behind few IOPS.

So the question for any dataset is: how many requests per second does each terabyte of it receive? If the answer is above what the dense tier offers, around 20 IOPS per TB for f4, placing it there would overload the disks and latency would suffer. If below, it can move safely and save money.

This is why hot data needs flash or well-spread HDD. Spreading hot data thinly across many disks gives each terabyte more IOPS, at the cost of wasted capacity. Cooling data can be packed densely. It also explains why the same principle appears in Colossus, which tries to keep disks both full and busy by pairing IOPS-hungry hot data with capacity-hungry cold data.

quiz.q: Why could data move to f4's warm tier only after its requests per TB dropped below about 20?
quiz.a: f4's 4 TB disks served about 80 IOPS, roughly 20 per TB; denser data with higher request rates would overload the disks and hurt latency.

title: Senior lens: temperature is IOPS per TB, age is only a proxy
body: Temperature is a property of IOPS per TB, not of age. Age is only a proxy that often correlates with access. Meta measured when each BLOB type's near-worst-case load, the 99th percentile, dropped below warm-tier capacity, and set the cutoff per type. When you design tiering, measure access per type and per age bucket. Do not pick 30 days just because a cloud console suggests it as a default.
deeper:
Using the 99th percentile rather than the average matters. Averages hide spikes: a type might average well below warm capacity yet regularly burst above it, and when it does, latency collapses for everyone sharing those disks. Sizing to near-worst-case load keeps the warm tier safe during bursts.

Per-type measurement matters because types cool at different rates. Profile photos never cooled enough; ordinary photos needed three months; most types needed one. A single global cutoff would either move profile photos too early and overload warm disks or keep other types hot too long and waste money.

The warning about defaults is practical. Cloud consoles and lifecycle templates often suggest round numbers like 30 days. Those are starting points, not facts about your workload. The same lens reappears later as a design-review question: ask for the access histogram, meaning bytes read in the last 7, 30, 90 and 365 days by object age, before accepting any tiering plan. Without measurement, tiering is guessing.

quiz.q: Why did Meta set tiering cutoffs using 99th-percentile load per BLOB type instead of a single average-based age?
quiz.a: Averages hide bursts that would overload warm disks, and types cool at different rates, so per-type near-worst-case load gives safe, cost-effective cutoffs.

title: Hot, warm, cold, archive: four tiers of storage
body: Storage tiering means storing data on different classes of media or service depending on how often it is read, and moving it between them over time. Common names: Hot data is read often and needs millisecond latency and high IOPS, on flash or well-spread HDD. Warm data is read sometimes but still needs fast first byte, on dense HDD, often more aggressively erasure-coded. Cold data is read rarely, on very dense HDD, sometimes powered down. Archive data is almost never read.
deeper:
Archive is the fourth tier: data read almost never, where retrieval in hours is fine. It lives on tape, powered-off disks or optical media.

Each step down trades performance for cost along several axes at once. Media gets denser, with fewer IOPS per TB. Redundancy gets leaner, using wider erasure codes instead of replicas, as in Meta's move from Haystack's 3.6x effective replication to f4's 2.8x and then 2.1x. Power use drops, sometimes to zero when drives are spun down or tapes sit on shelves. Access latency rises from milliseconds to minutes or hours.

The key phrase is first byte, the delay before data starts arriving. Warm storage still needs fast first byte, meaning readers do not wait noticeably. Cold and archive tiers relax that. Knowing which tier a dataset needs therefore comes down to two questions: how often it is read, measured as IOPS per TB, and how long a reader can tolerate waiting for the first byte when it is read.

quiz.q: What distinguishes warm from archive storage in terms of what readers can tolerate?
quiz.a: Warm data still needs fast first byte on dense HDD; archive data is almost never read, so retrieval taking hours from tape or powered-off disks is acceptable.

title: Two ways to tier: hidden inside the system or sold as classes
body: There are two ways to tier. First, inside the storage system, transparently: the system moves data between media or encodings on its own. Colossus puts hot data on flash and cooling data on disk, and Meta moved warm photos from Haystack (3.6x effective replication) to f4 (2.8x, then 2.1x). Second, exposed to the customer: cloud providers sell tiers as storage classes with different prices, chosen by the customer or by an automated feature.
deeper:
The two approaches put the decision in different hands. In transparent tiering, the operator sees actual access rates and can move data based on IOPS per TB, as Meta did with f4. Users never make choices, and there are no retrieval fees to optimize around, because the provider owns both the fleet and the bill.

In exposed tiering, the customer decides, either manually or via features like S3 Intelligent-Tiering and GCS Autoclass. The provider signals costs through prices: cheaper storage per GB, but retrieval fees, minimum durations and slower first byte. The customer must understand their access patterns to choose well, which is why break-even math matters.

Meta's Haystack-to-f4 move shows what transparent tiering can save. Dropping effective replication from 3.6x to 2.1x means each byte of warm data needs far less raw disk. Given that f4's data showed more than 80% of objects were warm, applying lower overhead to that majority saved a large share of total storage.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between transparent tiering and tiering exposed as storage classes?
quiz.a: Transparent tiering lets the storage system move data itself using its own access data; exposed tiering makes customers choose priced classes with retrieval fees and minimums.

title: Every cooler tier: cheaper storage, pricier reads, minimum stay
body: Every cooler storage tier makes the same deal: cheaper to store, more expensive to read, and a minimum stay. If you delete early, you still pay for the remaining days. Amazon S3 list prices in US East (N. Virginia), checked in 2026, illustrate this: Standard costs 0.023 dollars per GB-month for the first 50 TB, down to 0.021, while Glacier Deep Archive costs 0.0018, about 1 dollar per TB-month, with 12 to 48 hours to first byte.
deeper:
The full S3 ladder, per GB-month: Standard 0.023 down to 0.021, no retrieval fee, millisecond first byte, no minimum. Standard-IA 0.0125, per-GB retrieval fee, milliseconds, 30-day minimum. One Zone-IA 0.01, per-GB fee, milliseconds, 30 days. Glacier Instant Retrieval 0.004, per-GB fee, milliseconds, 90 days. Glacier Flexible Retrieval 0.0036, per-GB fee with bulk retrieval free, minutes to hours, 90 days. Glacier Deep Archive 0.0018, per-GB fee, 12 to 48 hours, 180 days.

Glacier Flexible Retrieval offers three speeds: expedited in 1 to 5 minutes, standard in 3 to 5 hours, and free bulk in 5 to 12 hours.

The ratio is striking: Standard to Deep Archive is about 12 to 13 times cheaper per GB. But reading 1 GB back from a cool tier can cost as much as storing it for months. So tiering saves money only when data really is cold. Minimum durations add a trap: moving data to a cold class and deleting it soon after means paying for the full minimum anyway.

quiz.q: Why can moving data to a cooler S3 class increase costs even though storage is cheaper?
quiz.a: Retrieval fees can equal months of storage per read, and minimum durations charge for remaining days if deleted early, so it only pays for truly cold data.

title: Standard-IA break-even: read more than once a month and it loses
body: When does S3 Standard-IA pay off? It saves about 0.0105 dollars per GB-month over Standard (0.023 minus 0.0125). Its retrieval fee is about 0.01 dollars per GB. So if an object is read in full more than about once per month, IA costs more than Standard. For a photo archive where photos older than three months are read far less than monthly, IA wins easily. For an analytics table scanned daily, it loses badly.
deeper:
The calculation generalizes to any tier: compare monthly storage savings per GB against expected monthly retrieval cost per GB. Break-even reads per month roughly equal the savings divided by the retrieval fee. For IA, 0.0105 divided by 0.01 is about one full read per month.

Worked example from the chapter's quiz: an object read in full twice a month. Savings are about 0.0105 dollars per GB-month, but two reads cost about 2 x 0.01 = 0.02 dollars per GB. IA costs nearly double the savings, so keep it in Standard.

This is why the chapter's takeaways say to do the break-even math per data type. The same bucket can hold data that belongs in different tiers: old photos that are rarely viewed and derived tables scanned every morning. Minimum durations add another factor: IA's 30-day minimum means short-lived objects pay for a full month regardless. With an access histogram per type, these calculations become straightforward instead of guesses.

quiz.q: An object in S3 Standard-IA is read in full twice per month. Is IA cheaper than Standard? Show the math.
quiz.a: No. IA saves about $0.0105/GB-month, but two reads cost about 2 x $0.01 = $0.02/GB. IA costs more; keep it in Standard.

title: Azure archive is offline; GCS Archive answers in milliseconds
body: Azure and Google offer the same tier shape as S3. Azure Blob Storage has hot, cool, cold and archive tiers: cool has a 30-day minimum, cold 90 days, archive 180 days. Azure archive is offline: a blob must be rehydrated, copied back to an online tier, before it can be read, which can take up to 15 hours. Google Cloud Storage has Standard, Nearline, Coldline and Archive, and GCS Archive is still online, with millisecond first byte.
deeper:
The key difference is whether the coldest tier is online. Azure archive, like S3 Glacier Deep Archive, is effectively offline: you must request data and wait hours before reading. Rehydration takes up to 15 hours, and applications must be designed to issue a request and come back later.

Google takes a different approach. GCS Archive keeps millisecond first byte, so reading archived data works like reading any other object. You pay for that convenience with higher retrieval fees and a 365-day minimum storage duration, twice Azure's and S3 Deep Archive's 180 days.

Azure charges early deletion pro-rata, so deleting archived data before its minimum means paying for the remaining days, the same minimum-stay trap as S3. Choosing between these depends on your read pattern. If archived data is truly never read except in disasters, an offline tier with slow retrieval is fine. If occasional reads must be immediate, an online archive like GCS's avoids redesigning applications around delayed retrieval, at a price.

quiz.q: What is the trade-off of GCS Archive being online compared with Azure's offline archive tier?
quiz.a: GCS Archive gives millisecond reads without rehydration but charges higher retrieval fees and a 365-day minimum; Azure archive needs up to 15 hours rehydration.

title: Lifecycle rules: after N days, move to class X or delete
body: A lifecycle rule is a policy on a storage bucket that says: after N days, move objects matching this prefix or tag to class X, or after M days, delete them. It runs automatically in the background. A typical S3 rule for event logs keeps events in Standard for 30 days, moves them to Standard-IA, then to Glacier Instant Retrieval at 90 days, to Deep Archive at 365 days, and deletes them after 2,555 days.
deeper:
In the chapter's running example, the rule is scoped with a filter on the prefix events/, and has three transitions plus an expiration. Its effect: events stay hot for a month, warm until 90 days, instantly readable until one year, then move to deep archive, and are deleted after about 7 years (2,555 days).

The shape follows the evidence about cooling: logs are read heavily right after they arrive, occasionally in the following weeks, and very rarely after that. Glacier Instant Retrieval between 90 and 365 days keeps millisecond access for the odd investigation while charging much less than Standard. Deep Archive handles the long tail at about 1 dollar per TB-month.

The expiration is as important as the transitions. It encodes a retention decision, deleting data when it is no longer needed, which saves more than any tier. Lifecycle rules are also the mechanism that platforms use to apply retention policies, translating a catalog of data types and their allowed ages into automatic transitions and deletes.

quiz.q: What does the expiration in the example event-log lifecycle rule accomplish that transitions alone do not?
quiz.a: It deletes events after about 7 years, enforcing retention; transitions only make storage cheaper, while deletion removes the cost and risk entirely.

title: Lifecycle traps: transition fees, tiny objects, age isn't access
body: Lifecycle rules are simple but have three traps. First, transition requests cost money: each object moved is a billed request, so billions of small objects can make transitions expensive. Second, very small objects may cost more in a cool class because of per-object overhead and minimum billable sizes, so batch them first. Third, age is not access: lifecycle rules move data by how old it is, not by whether anyone actually reads it.
deeper:
The first two traps both come from per-object costs. A lifecycle transition is billed per object, not per byte, so a bucket of billions of tiny log files can cost more to move than the storage savings justify. Cool classes also often charge minimum billable sizes and per-object overhead, which inflates the effective price of tiny objects. The fix is to combine small objects into larger ones, the same remedy as for the small-files problem, before tiering.

The third trap is conceptual. A lifecycle rule assumes old data is cold, but that is only a proxy. An old dataset that a monthly report scans will be moved to IA and then rack up retrieval fees, while a new object nobody reads stays in expensive Standard for 30 days. This echoes the earlier senior lens: temperature is IOPS per TB, not age.

The age-versus-access gap led providers to build access-based tiering, such as S3 Intelligent-Tiering and GCS Autoclass, which watch actual reads.

quiz.q: Why can lifecycle transitions be surprisingly expensive for a bucket of billions of small log files?
quiz.a: Each transition is a billed per-object request, and cool classes add per-object overhead and minimum billable sizes, so costs scale with object count, not bytes.

title: S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves each object by actual access
body: S3 Intelligent-Tiering fixes the age-is-not-access problem by watching each object. After 30 days without access it moves to an Infrequent Access tier; after 90 days, to Archive Instant Access. Optional Archive Access (after at least 90 days) and Deep Archive Access (after at least 180 days) tiers can be enabled for data that tolerates retrieval delays. When an object in the Infrequent or Archive Instant tier is read, it moves back to Frequent Access automatically.
deeper:
The pricing model is the key difference from lifecycle rules. Intelligent-Tiering has no retrieval fee. Instead it charges a monitoring fee of 0.0025 dollars per 1,000 objects per month. This removes the risk of retrieval fees exploding if a dataset turns out to be read more than expected, since reading simply moves an object back to Frequent Access.

There is an important exception: objects smaller than 128 KB are not monitored and always stay in Frequent Access. Tiny objects therefore get no benefit, another reason to batch small files.

The monitoring fee is per object, so it favors fewer, larger objects. For a bucket of billions of tiny objects, monitoring could be expensive or pointless. The flow can be pictured as a decision loop: an object written to the Frequent tier is checked for reads in the last 30 days; if none, it drops to Infrequent; if no reads in 90 days, to Archive Instant; optionally further to Archive or Deep Archive after 90 to 180+ days. Any read sends it back up.

quiz.q: How does S3 Intelligent-Tiering avoid the retrieval-fee risk of lifecycle rules?
quiz.a: It charges a per-object monitoring fee instead of retrieval fees, and a read automatically moves an object back to Frequent Access.

title: GCS Autoclass and Azure smart tier: Google's and Microsoft's take
body: GCS Autoclass does for Google what Intelligent-Tiering does for S3. Objects move to Nearline after 30 days without access, to Coldline after 90 days, and to Archive after 365 days if Archive is enabled as the terminal class. Reading an object's data moves it back to Standard. Objects under 128 KiB stay in Standard. Autoclass charges a management fee but no retrieval or early-deletion fees. Azure has lifecycle management policies and, more recently, a smart tier.
deeper:
Azure's smart tier moves data between hot, cool and cold automatically, the same idea as Autoclass and Intelligent-Tiering applied to Azure's tiers. Combined with Azure's lifecycle management policies, it offers both age-based and access-based options.

The chapter's comparison table summarizes the approaches. Lifecycle rules move by age, prefix and tag, charge retrieval fees, and suit predictable data like logs and backups. S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves per object by access, with a monitoring fee instead of retrieval fees, and suits unknown or mixed access. GCS Autoclass is the same, with a management fee. Internal tiering, as in Colossus or f4, moves by access and IOPS per TB, has no retrieval fees because it is the provider's own fleet, and is used there.

The rule of thumb follows: if you know your access pattern, lifecycle rules are cheaper and simpler; if you do not, access-based tiering avoids surprises. Both ignore small objects under about 128 KB, which is a key limitation noted in the takeaways.

quiz.q: When are plain lifecycle rules a better choice than access-based tiering like Autoclass?
quiz.a: When data is predictable, like logs or backups, age reliably tracks access, so you avoid monitoring or management fees on every object.

title: Senior lens: demand the access histogram before any tiering
body: In a design review, ask for the access histogram: for each data type, how many bytes were read in the last 7, 30, 90 and 365 days, grouped by object age. Without it, tiering is guessing. With it, you can compute the break-even point for each tier: whether retrieval fees, minimum durations and monitoring fees are outweighed by the storage savings for that specific data type. It turns tiering from opinion into arithmetic.
deeper:
The histogram is the concrete form of the earlier principle that temperature is IOPS per TB, not age. Grouping reads by object age shows how quickly each type cools, just as Meta's f4 study did for its nine BLOB types. Grouping by type prevents one global rule from mistreating data that behaves differently, like profile photos versus attachments.

The time windows map to tier decisions. Reads in the last 7 days show what is truly hot. The 30- and 90-day windows line up with typical minimum durations and the thresholds used by Intelligent-Tiering and Autoclass. The 365-day window reveals whether anything is read after a year, which determines whether deep archive or even deletion is appropriate.

With those numbers, you can apply the Standard-IA break-even: if bytes in a type are read in full more than about once a month, IA loses. You can also spot types where most bytes are never read at all, which raises the more valuable question from the retention section: why keep them?

quiz.q: Why group the access histogram by object age and data type rather than using one overall read rate?
quiz.a: Types cool at different speeds, and age grouping shows when each crosses tier break-evens; a single average hides both and leads to wrong cutoffs.

title: Archival: keep it for decades, read it almost never
body: Archival is storage for data you must keep but expect almost never to read. Examples include backups, legal holds, raw sensor data, old media masters and financial records. The goals are lowest cost per TB-year, very high durability and long media life. Latency measured in hours is acceptable. Because reads are so rare, archives can use slow media like tape, powered-down disks or experimental glass, trading access speed for cost and longevity.
deeper:
Archival differs from cold storage mainly in expectations. Cold data might be read occasionally; archive data is kept primarily as insurance or for obligations, such as a court order, a regulator, or a disaster recovery plan.

That changes what matters. Cost per TB-year, rather than per GB-month, reflects the long horizons involved. Durability must be very high because data may sit untouched for decades, and nobody will notice corruption unless something checks. Media life matters because a medium that fails or becomes unreadable in five years forces repeated copying, which the chapter calls the hidden archive cost.

Latency in hours opens design space. Robots can fetch tapes, drives can stay powered off until needed, reads can be batched, and entire datacenters can be built without backup power, as Meta did for cold storage. The options surveyed next range from cloud archive services with prices near 1 dollar per TB-month, through tape and powered-down disks, to Microsoft's research on glass.

quiz.q: Why is 'cost per TB-year' a better metric than 'cost per GB-month' for archival storage?
quiz.a: Archive data is kept for years or decades, so total long-horizon cost, including durability and media life, matters more than a short monthly price.

title: Cloud archive services and the mystery of their media
body: The main cloud archive services differ in speed and minimums. Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive: 12 to 48 hours to first byte, about 1 dollar per TB-month, 180-day minimum, launched 2019. Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval: minutes to 12 hours, 0.0036 dollars per GB-month, the original Glacier service launched 2012. Google Cloud Storage Archive: milliseconds, online, 365-day minimum. Azure Blob Archive: up to 15 hours to rehydrate, offline, 180-day minimum.
deeper:
A notable caution: AWS, Google and Microsoft do not publish which media their archive tiers use. Be careful with blog posts that claim to know. The service shape only tells us something indirect: retrieval delays of hours leave room for robotic media like tape libraries, powered-down drives, or batching many reads together before touching the media.

This matters for accuracy in design discussions. It is tempting to assume that Glacier is tape, for example, but that is not publicly confirmed. What you can reason about is the service contract: first-byte latency, minimum duration, storage price and retrieval fees.

The contrast between GCS Archive and the others is also a design signal. Millisecond first byte means the data is on media that can be read quickly, while Azure and Deep Archive's hours-long delays imply the provider can use slower, cheaper arrangements. Choosing a service is about matching that contract to how, and how urgently, you expect to read your archive, and to how long you will keep it given the minimums.

quiz.q: What can you actually infer about the media behind cloud archive tiers?
quiz.a: Only indirect clues: providers don't publish media, but hours-long retrieval leaves room for robotic media like tape, powered-down drives, or batched reads.

title: Tape: cheap, powerless on a shelf, and air-gapped
