body: Magnetic tape, today mostly LTO (Linear Tape-Open), is the oldest archive media still in wide use. It has three strengths: very low cost per TB of media; no power needed while a cartridge sits on a shelf; and an air gap, meaning a cartridge in a library slot cannot be deleted by ransomware or a software bug. Its weakness is access time: a robot loads the cartridge and the drive winds to the right spot.
deeper:
Loading and winding takes tens of seconds to minutes, far too slow for anything interactive but fine for archives where hours are acceptable.

The air gap is tape's most distinctive strength. Online systems, however well replicated, can be reached by software. A malicious actor or buggy code with write access can delete or encrypt every online copy. A cartridge sitting in a slot is physically disconnected, so nothing can alter it until it is loaded.

The market is still growing. The LTO Program reported 152.9 EB of new LTO capacity shipped in 2023 and 176.5 EB in 2024; these are compressed-capacity figures, meaning they assume data compression and overstate raw capacity. LTO-10 was introduced in 2025.

The main risk, per the chapter's media comparison, is that drive generations become obsolete. An LTO drive reads only a few generations back, so data on old cartridges must eventually be copied forward to newer media, part of the hidden migration cost of any archive.

quiz.q: What does tape's air gap protect against that replicated online storage cannot?
quiz.a: A cartridge sitting in a slot is disconnected, so ransomware or buggy software cannot delete or corrupt it, unlike online replicas software can reach.

title: Gmail 2011: a bug wiped replicas, tape brought mail back
body: Public evidence of tape inside hyperscalers is limited. The best-known case is Google. In February 2011, a software bug deleted Gmail data for a small share of users. Google restored it from tape backups, and its blog said it backs Gmail up to tape to protect against exactly such bugs. The lesson: replicas protect against hardware loss, but a software bug replicates instantly to every copy. Only an offline, separate copy protects against that.
deeper:
This incident is the clearest illustration of why replication is not backup. Replication keeps multiple synchronized copies so that a failed disk, server or even datacenter does not lose data. But synchronization works both ways: if software deletes or corrupts data, that change propagates to every replica, often within seconds. All copies are then equally wrong.

An offline copy breaks that chain. Because tapes are written separately and sit disconnected, the bug cannot reach them. Restoring from tape is slow, which is why Google's post described Gmail as back soon rather than immediately, but it is possible.

The chapter points to its later backup chapter for more on this. The practical takeaway for design reviews: when someone says data is safe because it has three replicas, ask what happens if the application deletes it. Replicas and erasure coding answer the hardware question; only separate, preferably air-gapped copies answer the software question. Features like S3 Object Lock provide a similar protection by blocking deletion until a set date.

quiz.q: Why couldn't Gmail's replicas protect against the 2011 data-deletion bug?
quiz.a: A software bug's deletions replicate instantly to every copy; only a separate, offline copy like tape was untouched and could restore the data.

title: Meta's cold storage halls: one exabyte, a sixth of the power
body: Meta, then Facebook, built dedicated cold storage datacenters in Prineville, Oregon and Forest City, North Carolina, described in 2015. Each data hall could hold up to one exabyte while using less than one-sixth of the power of Meta's normal datacenters. UPS systems and generators were removed entirely, because cold data can wait if power fails. Only one drive per tray was powered on at a time, cutting power per rack dramatically.
deeper:
A rack held 2 PB on 4 TB drives and used about one-quarter the power of normal storage servers. With most drives spun down, both power draw and cooling needs fall sharply.

Durability came from software rather than hardware redundancy. Reed-Solomon coding stored each 1 GB as 10 data chunks plus 4 parity chunks, 1.4 GB in total, so data survives the loss of any 4 chunks. A scanner checked every drive about every 30 days for silent corruption, bit rot that no one would otherwise notice because the data is rarely read.

Removing UPS and generators was safe because availability was not the goal. If power fails, cold data is temporarily unreachable, but nobody urgently needs it, and erasure coding across drives and racks keeps it durable even when some hardware is offline. In the media comparison, powered-down HDD access takes seconds to minutes, uses almost no power at rest, lasts about 5 years, and its main risk is a drive failing to spin up.

quiz.q: Why did Meta remove UPS and generators from its cold storage datacenters, and what made this safe?
quiz.a: Cold data can wait for power to return, so constant availability wasn't needed; erasure coding across drives and racks kept data durable with hardware offline.

title: Design the whole datacenter for one temperature
body: Meta's cold storage is a good example of designing an entire datacenter for one data temperature. By accepting that cold data can wait, Meta removed power redundancy, powered most drives off, and cut power per rack. The software made these hardware compromises safe: erasure coding protected against unavailable or failed drives, and read scheduling directed requests to the one drive powered on in each tray. Hardware and software were designed together around the workload.
deeper:
The general principle is that relaxing one requirement can unlock savings everywhere else. Normal datacenters are built for constant availability: redundant power, every drive spinning, low latency. Cold data does not need any of that, so a facility built only for cold data can shed all that cost.

The software side is what makes the bargain work. Because only one drive per tray is powered at a time, reads must be scheduled so the system powers the right drive and batches requests rather than thrashing between drives. Erasure coding with 10 data plus 4 parity chunks means data survives drives that are off, failed or unreachable. The 30-day scanner catches silent corruption before it accumulates beyond what parity can repair.

This mirrors tiering logic at a larger scale. Where tiering moves data to cheaper media, Meta built cheaper buildings. It also connects to the archive theme: the longer and colder the data, the more you can trade access speed for cost, provided durability is handled carefully in software.

quiz.q: How did software make Meta's cold-storage hardware compromises safe?
quiz.a: Erasure coding tolerated offline or failed drives, a scanner caught silent corruption, and reads were scheduled to the single powered drive per tray.

title: Meta's Blu-ray rack: a prototype, not a proven product
body: Meta also showed a Blu-ray optical disc cold storage rack as a prototype at the Open Compute Summit in 2014, pitched as cheaper and lower-power than disk-based cold storage. The chapter could not find a primary Meta source with verified capacity and savings figures, so it does not repeat numbers that circulated in the press. Optical should be treated as an experiment: Meta did not publish long-term production results for it.
deeper:
The chapter adds that Meta's later FAST 2021 paper describes Tectonic as the system that replaced Haystack and f4 for blob storage, with no mention of optical as a production tier. That is further reason to see the Blu-ray rack as a prototype rather than a lasting part of Meta's storage hierarchy.

In the archive media comparison, optical (Blu-ray prototype) has access times of seconds to minutes, uses no power at rest, claims media life of decades, and its main risks are low density and limited adoption.

The broader lesson is about evidence. Storage media claims often spread through press coverage and blog posts with numbers that cannot be traced to a primary source. The chapter deliberately withholds such figures, the same caution it applies to claims about which media cloud archive tiers use. When evaluating archive technology, prefer published production results and papers over demos and announcements, and treat unsupported figures as unverified. A prototype shows possibility; long-term production data shows viability.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter treat Meta's Blu-ray cold storage rack as an experiment rather than a proven design?
quiz.a: No primary Meta source verifies capacity or savings, no long-term production results were published, and Tectonic later replaced its blob stores without optical.

title: Project Silica: writing data into glass with lasers
body: Project Silica is Microsoft Research's work on storing data in quartz glass. A femtosecond laser, one with extremely short pulses, writes tiny 3D changes called voxels in layers inside a glass platter. A microscope reads them using polarized light, and machine learning decodes the image back into bits. The glass is expected to last thousands of years or more, so data would never need copying to new media. It is research, not a product.
deeper:
Microsoft has published several facts. A platter about the size of a DVD has raw capacity above 7 TB. Magnetic media requires copying data to new media every 5 to 10 years, but glass is expected to last thousands of years, removing that need. A 2023 SOSP paper described a full library design with separate read, write and storage racks and robotic shuttles moving platters between them. Once written, glass cannot be overwritten. The design met a 15-hour service level objective for archive reads, even with read drives of only 30 MB/s. A proof of concept with Warner Bros. was announced in 2019.

The write-once property is a double-edged feature: it protects against accidental or malicious modification, similar to tape's air gap, but means deletions must be handled differently. The separation of read, write and storage racks means expensive writers and readers are shared across many passive platters. Silica shows where archive design is going: media needing no power, no refresh and no migration.

quiz.q: How does the Silica library meet a 15-hour read SLO despite read drives of only 30 MB/s?
quiz.a: Archive reads are rare, so separate read racks and robotic shuttles bring platters to shared drives; a 15-hour objective leaves ample time.

title: Archive media head to head: disk, tape, optical, glass
body: Four archive media compared. Powered-down HDD, as in Meta's cold storage: seconds to minutes access, almost no power at rest, about 5 years of life, main risk a drive failing to spin up. Tape (LTO): tens of seconds to minutes, no power, decades if stored well, risk that drive generations become obsolete. Optical (Blu-ray prototype): seconds to minutes, no power, claimed decades, low density and limited adoption. Glass (Silica research): hours in the library design, no power, thousands of years claimed, not yet a product.
deeper:
Reading across the table reveals the real trade-offs. Access time varies but is always slow compared with online storage, which is fine for archives. Power at rest is nearly zero for all of them, which is the core cost advantage over spinning disks.

The differences lie in lifetime and risk. Powered-down disks are the most familiar technology but have the shortest life, about 5 years, and a drive that has been idle may fail to spin up when finally needed. Tape lasts decades physically, but the practical limit is readers: drives read only a few generations back. Optical claims long life but never achieved wide adoption or high density. Glass claims the longest life by far but is research.

The common thread is that media life alone is not enough; you also need working readers. That is why the next idea, migration cost, dominates long-term archive economics. The Main risk column is the most useful for design reviews, because it names what will actually cause data loss or expense decades from now.

quiz.q: Tape cartridges can last decades. Why is that not enough to avoid copying tape archives?
quiz.a: LTO drives read only a few generations back, so readers become obsolete before the media wears out, forcing migration to newer formats.

section: 7.6.6 Migration is the hidden archive cost
title: Migration: the hidden cost that eats archive budgets
body: Archive readers become obsolete. An LTO drive reads only a few generations back, and hard drives last about five years. So an archive must be re-copied to new media several times over a 30-year retention period. At exabyte scale, each migration is a major project: reading everything back, writing it to new media, and verifying it. The cloud provider handling this for you is a big reason cloud archive is attractive.
deeper:
Removing migration is the main promise of glass storage like Project Silica, whose platters are expected to last thousands of years, so data can be written once and never migrated.

The cost is hidden because it does not appear when you first store data. The price per TB-month on day one does not include the future labor, hardware and risk of copying everything forward every five to ten years. Over a long retention period, those migrations can rival or exceed the media cost itself.

Migrations also carry risk: every copy is a chance to lose or corrupt data, and they compete for the same limited read throughput archives are designed around. A 30-year retention on media lasting 5 to 10 years means three to six full migrations.

This changes the build-versus-buy calculation. A company running its own tape archive must plan and staff these migrations; a cloud archive customer pays a monthly price and the provider absorbs them. When comparing archive options, include migration in the total cost of ownership.

quiz.q: Why is media migration a hidden cost of archival, and how does Project Silica aim to remove it?
quiz.a: Magnetic media lasts about 5 to 10 years and readers become obsolete, forcing repeated copies; glass lasts thousands of years, so data is written once and never migrated.

title: Retention: a minimum from law, a maximum from privacy and cost
body: Tiering decides where data lives; retention decides how long it lives. A retention policy is a rule stating how long each type of data must be kept, the minimum, and when it must be deleted, the maximum. Both limits matter. Minimum retention comes from law and business: financial records, audit logs, legal holds. Maximum retention comes from privacy law and cost: every day you keep unneeded data costs money and increases breach risk.
deeper:
GDPR's storage-limitation principle means personal data should not be kept longer than needed, which makes maximum retention a legal requirement for personal data, not just a cost optimization.

The chapter describes a typical flow for enforcing retention. Data is created with a type tag. A retention catalog maps each type to its minimum and maximum days. The platform applies lifecycle rules and TTLs (time to live) based on that catalog. Before deleting, it checks whether a legal hold is active. If yes, it keeps the data and blocks deletion. If no, data is tiered down over time, then deleted at its maximum age, and the deletion is recorded in an audit log.

In the running example, raw click events might be deleted after 2 years for cost and privacy, audit logs kept 7 years for compliance, and photos kept until the user deletes them, per the user contract. These are illustrative, not legal advice. For the minimum side, S3 Object Lock and Azure immutable blob storage block deletion until a date.

quiz.q: Where do the minimum and maximum limits of a retention policy come from?
quiz.a: Minimums come from law and business needs like financial records, audits and legal holds; maximums come from privacy law such as GDPR plus cost and breach risk.

title: Object Lock and immutable blobs: enforcing the minimum
body: For the minimum side of retention, providers offer immutability features such as S3 Object Lock and Azure immutable blob storage. These block deletion of data until a set date, so nothing, not a mistaken script, a careless administrator or ransomware, can remove it early. They protect against both human mistakes and malicious deletion, making retention minimums a technical guarantee rather than a policy that depends on everyone following the rules.
deeper:
Immutability features complement the retention flow. When the platform's catalog says audit logs must be kept 7 years, a lock can ensure that no one, including those with write access, can delete them before the date. Legal holds work similarly: while a hold is active, data is kept and deletion is blocked.

The protection against ransomware is significant. Ransomware typically encrypts or deletes data and demands payment; if the data cannot be deleted or overwritten until a date, the attack cannot destroy those copies. This parallels tape's air gap and the Gmail lesson: replicas protect against hardware failure, but software, whether buggy or malicious, can reach every online copy unless something blocks it.

The flip side is that immutability must be applied carefully. Data locked for a long period cannot be removed to honor the maximum side of retention or a user's deletion request until the lock expires. Designing retention means setting both limits deliberately per data type, using the catalog, lifecycle rules, locks and audit logs together.

quiz.q: How do features like S3 Object Lock help against ransomware?
quiz.a: They block deletion or overwriting until a set date, so malicious software cannot destroy locked copies even with write access.

title: Common mistake: deleting raw data but not its copies
body: A common mistake is setting a deletion rule on the raw data but not on its copies. A deleted event still lives on in derived tables, ML training sets, backups and caches. Retention has to follow the lineage, the chain of datasets built from the original. Otherwise the policy is enforced on paper while the data survives elsewhere. LinkedIn's OpenHouse builds retention into the table platform itself for exactly this reason.
deeper:
Data in a lake rarely stays in one place. A single click event may flow into a sessionized table, then a daily active users table, an ad report and an ML training set, plus backups and caches along the way. Deleting it from the raw event log after 2 years accomplishes little if the derived copies persist indefinitely.

This matters for both cost and compliance. On cost, derived tables may be as large as the raw data. On compliance, privacy rules like GDPR's storage limitation apply to personal data wherever it lives, so a forgotten copy can still violate the maximum retention requirement.

Following lineage requires knowing what was derived from what, and applying policy consistently across all of it. That is hard to do team by team, which is why LinkedIn put retention, data purging and partition expiration into OpenHouse alongside compaction and snapshot expiration. When retention is a platform service, every table registered with it gets policies applied automatically, rather than depending on each team to remember.

quiz.q: Why doesn't deleting raw event data after 2 years fully enforce a retention policy?
quiz.a: Copies persist in derived tables, ML training sets, backups and caches; retention must follow lineage to every dataset built from the original.

title: Senior lens: the cheapest byte is the byte you deleted
body: The cheapest byte is the byte you deleted. Before building a clever tiering system, ask: why are we keeping this at all? At most companies, a retention review saves more than any tiering project. Tiering can cut storage cost by about 12 to 13 times at best between S3 Standard and Deep Archive, but deletion cuts it to zero and also removes breach risk, migration cost and compliance exposure.
deeper:
The comparison is stark once framed this way. Tiering reduces the price per byte; retention reduces the number of bytes. A dataset moved to Deep Archive still costs about 1 dollar per TB-month forever, still must be migrated to new media over decades, and still counts as stored personal data for privacy purposes. A deleted dataset costs nothing.

Tiering is also where engineering effort tends to go, because it is a technical challenge. Retention is a policy question that requires talking to legal, product and data owners, which is harder organizationally but often yields bigger savings.

The chapter's takeaways reinforce this: retention policies with both minimum and maximum limits, applied across all copies, save more money and risk than tiering alone. In practice, the two work together. The retention catalog sets how long each type lives; lifecycle rules tier data down during that window and delete it at the end. But the first question in any design review of a growing storage bill should be which data does not need to exist.

quiz.q: Why might a retention review save more than a sophisticated tiering project?
quiz.a: Tiering only lowers price per byte, while deletion removes bytes entirely, eliminating storage, migration, breach and compliance costs rather than just shrinking them.

title: Chapter 7 in ten lines: lakes, tiers, archives, retention
body: The chapter's core lessons: a data lake separates storage from compute, optimizing for cheap, high-throughput bytes. HDFS lakes hit NameNode memory and 3x replication limits; object stores remove those but lose locality and atomic rename, which table formats replace. Small files are permanent, so compaction must be a platform service. Data cools fast, and temperature means IOPS per TB. Cooler tiers need break-even math. Archive media wins on cost but hides migration costs. Retention beats tiering.
deeper:
Several company-specific takeaways anchor these lessons. Uber announced in 2024 a move of its more-than-1-exabyte Hadoop lake to Google Cloud, starting by swapping HDFS for GCS behind the same API. Meta instead replaced HDFS with its own Tectonic and cut warehouse clusters by 10 times. Meta's f4 data showed request rates falling 10 times within a week for most BLOB types, and more than 80% of objects warm in older intervals.

On tiering mechanics: move data to dense media when its access rate falls below what that media can serve. Cooler tiers trade lower storage prices for retrieval fees, minimum durations and slower first byte, so do the math per data type. Access-based tiering such as S3 Intelligent-Tiering and GCS Autoclass fixes the age-is-not-access problem but ignores objects under 128 KB.

On archives: tape, powered-down disk and glass research win on cost and power, but migrating to new media is a hidden long-term cost. On retention: set both minimum and maximum limits and apply them across all copies, since that saves more money and risk than tiering alone.

quiz.q: What limitation do S3 Intelligent-Tiering and GCS Autoclass share regarding small objects?
quiz.a: Objects under about 128 KB are not monitored or moved; they stay in the frequent or standard tier, so tiny files gain nothing.
